name: Ancient History – Mauryan Empire: Sources, Inscriptions, Arthashastra & Political History

notes.heading: Overview
points: Mauryan Empire (c. 322–185 BCE) was the first large centralized empire in India
Founded by Chandragupta Maurya with guidance of Chanakya (Kautilya)
Strong administrative system and extensive territorial control
Well-documented through inscriptions, archaeological sites, and literary texts

notes.heading: Sources of Mauryan History – Overview
points: Inscriptions (Ashokan edicts are the most important)
Indian literary sources (Arthashastra, Buddhist and Jain texts)

notes.heading: Inscriptions – Ashokan Edicts
points: Most important source for Mauryan history
Written in Prakrit using Brahmi and Kharosthi scripts
Major Rock Edicts and Pillar Edicts
Reflect Ashoka’s Dhamma policy and administration

notes.heading: Types of Ashokan Inscriptions
points: Major Rock Edicts – policy and moral instructions
Minor Rock Edicts – personal and religious details
Pillar Edicts – administrative and ethical guidelines
Help understand geography of Mauryan Empire

notes.heading: Archaeological Sites
points: Pataliputra – capital city with wooden fortifications
Sarnath – Ashokan pillar with lion capital
Kalinga – site of war and transformation of Ashoka

notes.heading: Foreign Accounts
points: Megasthenes – Greek ambassador to Chandragupta Maurya
Wrote Indica describing Mauryan society and administration
Mentioned seven-fold division of society (interpreted differently)
Described capital Pataliputra and its administration
Provides external perspective on Mauryan India

notes.heading: Literary Sources – Arthashastra
points: Treatise on statecraft, economy, and military strategy

notes.heading: Mauryan Rulers – Overview
points: Ashoka – greatest ruler, promoter of Dhamma

notes.heading: Chandragupta Maurya (322–297 BCE)
points: Founded Mauryan Empire by defeating Nandas
Defeated Seleucus Nicator in northwest India
Later became Jain monk and renounced throne

notes.heading: Ashoka (273–232 BCE)
points: Fought Kalinga War leading to transformation

notes.heading: Kalinga War
points: Resulted in massive destruction and loss of life
Led to adoption of non-violence policy

notes.heading: Ashoka’s Dhamma
points: Ethical and moral code of conduct

notes.heading: Decline of Mauryan Empire
points: Assassination of last Mauryan ruler Brihadratha

name: Ancient History – Megasthenes, Ashoka, Successors, Inscriptions & Ashokan Reign

notes.heading: Overview
points: Mauryan Empire under Ashoka is best documented ancient Indian period
Megasthenes provides important foreign account of Mauryan India
Ashoka’s inscriptions are the most reliable source of his reign
His successors marked the gradual decline of Mauryan power

notes.heading: Megasthenes – Overview
points: Greek ambassador of Seleucus Nicator to Chandragupta Maurya
Author of Indica (lost but quoted by later writers)
Gave foreign account of Indian society and administration

notes.heading: Megasthenes – Key Observations
points: Described Pataliputra as a large and well-fortified city
Mentioned seven-fold division of society (interpretation debated)
Noted absence of slavery in Indian society (possibly misunderstood)

notes.heading: Limitations of Megasthenes’ Account
points: Lack of understanding of Indian social structures
Lost original text; known through quotations

notes.heading: Ashoka – Introduction
points: Third ruler of Mauryan dynasty (273–232 BCE)
Initially expansionist, later turned to Dhamma
Fought Kalinga War leading to moral transformation

notes.heading: Ashoka and His Successors
points: Ashoka’s reign marked peak of Mauryan Empire
After his death, weak successors ruled
Empire gradually fragmented into regional powers

notes.heading: Important Successors of Ashoka
points: Later rulers had weak control over provinces

notes.heading: Ashoka’s Inscriptions – Overview
points: Most important source for Ashoka’s reign
Written in Prakrit using Brahmi and Kharosthi scripts
Found across Indian subcontinent and Afghanistan
Include Major Rock Edicts, Minor Rock Edicts, Pillar Edicts

notes.heading: Pillar Edicts
points: Famous example: Sarnath Lion Capital (national emblem)

notes.heading: Ashokan Sites
points: Sarnath – famous pillar and lion capital
Lumbini – birthplace of Buddha (inscribed by Ashoka)

notes.heading: Ashokan Reign – Administration
points: Empire divided into provinces governed by officials
Dhamma Mahamatras appointed for moral governance

notes.heading: Ashoka’s Dhamma Policy
points: Non-violence and compassion towards all beings

notes.heading: Importance of Ashokan Reign
points: First ruler to communicate directly with subjects via inscriptions
Model of welfare state in ancient India

name: Ancient History – Ashoka: Buddhism, Dhamma Policy, Mauryan Administration & Foreign Relations

notes.heading: Overview
points: Ashoka (273–232 BCE) was the most significant Mauryan ruler
His reign marked a shift from conquest to moral governance
Buddhism gained imperial support and global spread under him
Mauryan administration became highly centralized and efficient
Foreign relations expanded through peaceful and diplomatic channels

notes.heading: Ashoka and Buddhism
points: Ashoka adopted Buddhism after the Kalinga War
He became a lay follower (Upasaka) of Buddhism
Did not impose Buddhism as state religion
Promoted Buddhist ethics and moral values
Supported Sangha and sent missionaries abroad

notes.heading: Role in Spread of Buddhism
points: Sent missionaries to Sri Lanka, Central Asia, West Asia
Son Mahinda and daughter Sanghamitta spread Buddhism to Sri Lanka
Helped transform Buddhism into a world religion

notes.heading: Ashoka’s Dhamma Policy – Overview
points: Not a religion but a moral code of conduct
Based on ethical and social responsibilities
Aimed at harmony in a diverse empire

notes.heading: Principles of Dhamma
points: Respect for elders, parents, and teachers

notes.heading: Objectives of Dhamma
points: Social harmony in a diverse empire
Unification of empire through shared values

notes.heading: Dhamma Mahamatras
points: Looked after welfare of people and prisoners

notes.heading: Provincial Administration
points: Governed by royal princes or governors

notes.heading: Military Administration
points: Large standing army (infantry, cavalry, elephants, chariots)
Six boards or departments for military management

notes.heading: Revenue Administration
points: Land tax was main source of revenue
State controlled mines, forests, and trade

notes.heading: Foreign Relations – Overview
points: Mauryan Empire maintained diplomatic relations with Hellenistic kingdoms
Ashoka preferred peaceful diplomacy over warfare
Relations with Seleucid Empire, Egypt, and Sri Lanka

notes.heading: Relations with Hellenistic World
points: Trade relations with West Asia and Greece
Cultural exchange between India and Mediterranean world

notes.heading: Relations with Sri Lanka
points: Mission led by Mahinda and Sanghamitta
Sri Lankan king Devanampiya Tissa adopted Buddhism

notes.heading: Significance of Ashoka’s Policies
points: First attempt at welfare state governance in India
Strengthened internal unity of diverse empire
Model of non-violent leadership in ancient history

name: Ancient History – Decline of the Mauryan Empire

notes.heading: Overview
points: The Mauryan Empire declined after the death of Ashoka (232 BCE)
The empire weakened due to internal and external factors
Centralized administration became difficult to sustain
End of Mauryan rule marked by assassination of last ruler

notes.heading: Post-Ashokan Period
points: Successors of Ashoka were weak and ineffective
Empire began to fragment into provinces
Administrative control weakened over distant regions

notes.heading: Weak Successors
points: Later Mauryan rulers lacked political and military ability
Brihadratha was the last Mauryan emperor
Dependence on ministers and generals increased
No major expansion or reforms after Ashoka

notes.heading: Over-Centralization Problem
points: Heavy dependence on strong ruler (Ashoka’s model)

notes.heading: Economic Factors
points: Disruption in trade routes in some regions

notes.heading: Military Factors
points: Large army became difficult to maintain

notes.heading: Administrative Weakness
points: Lack of strong surveillance after Ashoka
Dhamma policy reduced focus on military expansion

notes.heading: Rise of Regional Powers
points: Deccan and South India remained outside control

notes.heading: External Factors
points: Loss of control over frontier areas

notes.heading: Final End of Mauryan Empire
points: Assassinated by his commander Pushyamitra Shunga
This marked end of Mauryan dynasty (c. 185 BCE)

notes.heading: Significance of Decline
points: Shift in political structure of India
Foundation for later dynasties like Shungas and Satavahanas
